I Can Just Build My Website With AI. Why Would I Hire You?

By Marie Glow StudioPublished September 28, 2026

Can AI build a website? Yes, seriously. It can write code, generate layouts, help with copy and create imagery, and I use AI myself. I'm not going to tell you to hire a web designer just because AI exists and I happen to build websites.

The question isn't whether AI can build your website. The question is whether you want to figure out everything the AI needs to get right. If you do, great. If you'd rather not, that's what the rest of this post is about.

Can AI build a website for a small business?

Yes. AI can write code, generate page layouts, help you write copy, suggest ideas when you're stuck, troubleshoot problems, create images, assist with research and speed up development. It can get you a first draft of a page very quickly. For a simple site where you already know what you want to say, that can be a perfectly good place to start.

Google doesn't rule it out either. Its guide to optimizing for generative AI features says that if you use generative AI tools, the work still has to meet Google's Search Essentials and spam policies, including the policy on scaled content abuse. As that guide describes it, Google's test is the quality of the work that comes out, not the tool that made it.

So I'm not here to argue that AI can't build websites. It can. What it can't do by itself is decide what to build.

What does AI still need a person to decide?

AI is a tool. It isn't the entire service, because somebody still has to make a long list of decisions before or while anything gets generated. If nobody makes them, the tool has to guess. Here is the list:

  • Who the site is for, and what a visitor needs to understand first
  • Which pages you actually need, and what order the information comes in
  • Where each page leads, whether that is a purchase, a booking or a quote request
  • What people search for, and which page should answer each search
  • How the site is organized and how its pages link to each other
  • How it works on a phone, and whether people using screen readers or keyboards can use it
  • Analytics, forms, integrations and the technical setup behind them
  • Which of the AI's output is good and which is garbage

The right answers change by business. A contractor's site has to make a quote request feel easy. A baker's has to make an order or a custom cake inquiry feel easy. An AI tool has no way to know which one you are unless someone tells it. If you run a service business, what a service business website needs covers that side in more detail.

A couple of these are more checkable than they sound. Google's guidance on asking Google to recrawl your pages says that requesting a crawl doesn't guarantee your pages will appear in search results instantly, or even at all. Google's AI guide also says SEO on sites built with JavaScript frameworks is generally more complex, which is worth asking about whenever any tool, or any person, picks the technology your site is built on.

And nobody can promise your site a mention in ChatGPT, Google's AI features or Perplexity. I won't, and be careful with anyone who does. What you control is clear, well organized pages, accurate business information and a site that search engines can read. Google's guide says the basics of SEO still hold for its AI features, so that work still counts.

But couldn't I ask AI all of that too?

Yes, honestly. You could ask an AI about every item on that list, and you could learn to do all of it: web design, SEO, conversion strategy, accessibility, analytics, development, prompting and testing. If you want to learn those things, please do. It's a great skill set and nothing about it is out of your reach.

Many owners didn't start a business to spend their evenings on it, though. A baker wants to bake. A stylist wants to be with clients. A maker wants to make things, and a spa owner wants to work with the people on the table. None of them are dreaming about spending Saturday night debugging a mobile navigation menu. I get it. I have seven kids and a life, and my evenings are already spoken for.

Paying someone to handle it is a reasonable use of money, and it says nothing about whether you could learn it. If you're weighing the two routes, DIY website vs professional website design lays out the trade-offs, and how much a small business website costs covers the money side.

Okay, but what about all the AI slop?

We've all seen it. The same glossy images, the same identical-looking people striking the same poses, everything a little too polished to be real. Layouts you've seen a hundred times, random gradients, sections nobody asked for, phrasing that repeats itself and brand language that sounds fake. Content that technically exists but says nothing.

I've made some of it too. Part of my experience with AI has been learning to use it better. I give the model real context instead of a vague request. I use references and brand guidelines so it isn't guessing, set constraints and keep the visuals consistent. I research before I generate, question the decisions the AI makes, rewrite generic output and regenerate weak work. I check facts, test what came back and have learned to spot the repetitive patterns. I also know when not to use AI at all, and when a human decision has to override the model.

Slop isn't the unavoidable result of using AI. It often comes from accepting what the tool gave you without enough direction, judgment or editing. Better direction doesn't remove every limit, which is why I check, test and rewrite, and why some decisions stay with a person.

Better AI starts with better direction

Someone can use the exact same AI tools I use and get a completely different result. Having access to a tool is not the same as knowing how to direct it.

Owning Canva doesn't make you a graphic designer. Owning Photoshop doesn't make you a retoucher, a good camera doesn't make you a photographer, and a heat press doesn't make a good print by itself. An AI model won't automatically make a good website either. The tool matters, and so do experience, taste and judgment.

Good direction sounds like this: here is the audience, here is what they ask before they buy, here is how the brand sounds, here is what's off the table, and here is a reference to match. When a version comes back off, someone has to know what is off and why.

You're not paying me to avoid AI

Marie Glow Studio isn't an anti-AI studio. I'm also not charging you because I possess some magical ability to type HTML that AI doesn't have.

What you're paying for is everything around the typing: strategy, research, direction, implementation, editing, quality control and troubleshooting. Someone has to know what to keep, what to change and what to throw away. A page can look finished and still be wrong for your customer, so someone also has to decide when the site is actually ready to represent your business. That work is invisible in a finished page, and it is the part you notice most when it is missing.

AI doesn't know your business until someone teaches it

An AI model starts your project knowing nothing about you. It doesn't know what you offer, who your competitors are, why people choose you, what makes customers hesitate or what you've already tried. It doesn't know what your brand sounds like when nobody is editing it, or what data you already have. You can feed it some of that, and I do, but somebody has to gather it first.

That's why my process starts with discovery, before anything gets built. I want to understand your business, your customers, your goals, what's wrong with your current site if you have one, your brand personality, the content you have and the content you still need, the search opportunities and the technical requirements. The about page describes the order I work in, with research coming before design.

AI can help carry out a strategy, but the strategy has to come from somewhere first. It's also why I don't make speed the promise, which I explain in can a website be built in a day.

How do I use AI in my own work?

I don't hide the fact that I use AI. I also don't pretend everything AI gives me is good. Where AI-generated content is part of a project, I'm transparent about it where that's appropriate, and wherever possible the work is built from real material: your actual business information, your real brand assets, real references, real research and human judgment about all of it.

I don't sit at either extreme. AI is an extremely capable tool. It can produce excellent work, and it can produce absolute garbage, and telling the two apart is part of the skill. If you'd rather judge by results, the portfolio has real work to look at.

So when does it make sense to hire someone?

If you want to build your own website with AI, do it. I'm genuinely not here to convince you that you can't. But if you reach the point where you're thinking, "Okay, I can technically build this, but I have no idea whether I'm building the right thing," that is where I come in.

If you need one professional page for a shop or a service business, the Website Starter is built for that. It's delivered in five business days from a completed intake. If you need branding and a full site together, the Complete Website and Brand Identity package is the fit. Its timeline is roughly two to three weeks, set mostly by how fast your content and images arrive. The web design and development overview compares both, and you can see everything else on the services page.

Not sure yet? The FAQs answer the AI question in short form, and you can ask me anything on the contact page. And if you build it yourself with AI and it turns out great, I'd honestly love to see it.

Frequently asked questions

Are AI website builders good enough for a small business website?

They can be for a simple site, when you give the tool clear direction and check what it produces. What decides the result is the information you bring: who the site is for, what visitors should see first, which pages you need and how people will find it. If you have those answers, an AI builder can be a reasonable start. If you are unsure you are building the right thing, that is a good time to ask a designer for help.

Will Google penalize my website because AI helped build it?

Not simply because AI was involved, going by Google's published guidance. Google's guide to generative AI features says that if you use AI tools, the work still has to meet its Search Essentials and spam policies, including the policy on scaled content abuse. The same guide says content people find unique, compelling and useful will likely matter more than any other suggestion in it. No one can promise rankings or a mention in an AI tool, whether the site was built by hand, with AI or both.

What should I check before publishing a website AI helped build?

In my experience it helps to check the facts the tool gave you, test what it produced, question the choices the AI made instead of accepting them, and rewrite anything that reads as generic. It also helps to watch for repeated patterns, such as the same phrasing or the same style of image over and over. These are habits I have built while learning to use AI better.

How can I tell if the copy on my website is generic?

Read a paragraph and ask whether a competitor could paste it onto their site without changing a word. Generic copy rarely names your actual services, products, town or customers, and it tends to use impressive words that leave you unsure what the business does. Replace those lines with specifics only you know, such as what you sell, who you serve and what customers ask you most often.
